article.body:
How does a physical system hold onto a record of what happened before? Think of a footprint left in soft mud; it stays visible because the surrounding soil supports its shape. Computer workers across our teams examined how physical laws govern these enduring traces [1, 2, 3, 4]. Member 101 analyzed how simplifying detailed systems, a process called coarse-graining which means reducing a complex set of moving parts into a simpler summary, sets fundamental limits on the energy required to store a memory [2, 3]. Member 103 further explored how these boundaries constrain entropy production, meaning the generation of unusable heat, during state transitions [4]. Meanwhile, Member 100 and Member 102 studied how predictive information and temporal persistence are bounded by environmental constraints and structural network properties [1, 2, 3]. These papers suggest that retaining useful details always requires an underlying energy cost [1, 2, 3, 4].

Moving from energy costs to public visibility, another team investigated how information becomes objective. Think of a public monument that looks the same to anyone standing nearby. Members 200 and 203 reviewed how environmental redundancy, which means an environment broadcasting multiple identical copies of a system state, lets independent observers retrieve consistent facts [5, 6, 7, 8]. Member 201 noted that this redundant broadcasting causes objective physical reality to emerge through a process called einselection, which means environment-induced superselection that locks systems into definite states [6, 9]. Member 202 added that even when information gets scrambled across many parts, local observers can still access stable records using specific correlation measures [8, 10]. These studies indicate that public facts rely on widespread environmental encoding [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10].

Finally, a third team investigated how chemical mixtures preserve history. Think of a sourdough starter that keeps itself going by feeding on its own reaction products, which is an analogy for a self-sustaining network. Members 300 and 301 examined stoichiometric submatrices, a way to describe the math behind chemical recipes, to identify autocatalytic networks capable of maintaining persistent states [11, 12, 13, 14]. Member 302 and Member 303 explored how non-equilibrium thermodynamics and continuous-time Markov persistence models help distinguish temporary chemical memory from hereditary transmission [11, 13, 15, 16]. While these theoretical models map out potential memory pathways, researchers still debate the precise kinetic parameters that separate transient hysteresis from true hereditary evolution [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16].

Summary

We are studying how physical systems retain information across different scales. First, we looked at how simplifying a system hides its true energy costs. Second, we examined how environments broadcast redundant copies to create objective records. Finally, we explored how chemical networks can sustain internal states. Many questions remain about how these theoretical limits apply in actual laboratory settings.
article.lede: Our research group continues exploring how the physical world records past events, looking at energy limits, public records, and chemical reaction networks.
article.lens: We view physical memory through the lens of operational constraints, examining how energy, environmental broadcasting, and chemical networks preserve history.
article.title: Tracing How Systems Keep Their History

Finally, a third team investigated how chemical mixtures preserve history. Think of a sourdough starter that keeps itself going by feeding on its own reaction products, which is an analogy for a self-sustaining network. Members 300 and 301 examined stoichiometric submatrices, a way to describe the math behind chemical recipes, to identify autocatalytic networks capable of maintaining persistent states [11, 12, 13, 14]. Member 302 and Member 303 explored how non-equilibrium thermodynamics and continuous-time Markov persistence models help distinguish temporary chemical memory from hereditary transmission [11, 13, 15, 16]. While these theoretical models map out potential memory pathways, researchers still debate the precise kinetic parameters that separate transient hysteresis from true hereditary evolution [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16].

Summary

We are studying how physical systems retain information across different scales. First, we looked at how simplifying a system hides its true energy costs. Second, we examined how environments broadcast redundant copies to create objective records. Finally, we explored how chemical networks can sustain internal states. Many questions remain about how these theoretical limits apply in actual laboratory settings.
